questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Studying in an English speaking country, the placement in a culturally rich city, the courses offered by the school, the academic level at the school and the warm weather.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was an amazing experience and I would definitely do it all over again. The area around the uptown campus where we lived was safe, but you had to be aware of safety measures when it was dark or when leaving the area surrounding the uptown campus. The university did inform us of this and taught us how to live in New Orleans. I didn't experience any crimes and neither did anyone i knew.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: We were sent several documents regarding the exchange. The university was always very quick at answering any questions. The documents necessary for applying for the visa came a bit late, so I had to apply as soon as they came.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I was enrolled in their intro course for exchange and LLM students, which started a month before the fall term. We received a lot of different assistance, such as practical measures (a tour of the campus, etc.), cultural experiences (a guided tour of the city, a field trip to the art museum, food, etc.) and information about the courses (setting up their exam software, how to get books, etc.).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: The orientation was very good and generally thorough. It was very clear that the university had a lot of resources, as it's a private university. I do wish that they had explained what the health care insurances covered.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
The university helped provide housing during the beginning of the intro summer course, but they did not provide housing after that. 

It was easy to find housing on your own. It's possible to find a lot of options in the Facebook groups "Tulane Classifieds" and "Tulane University (TU) Housing, Sublets & Roommates". We found our housing by making a post in there. 

The price of rent has gone up after COVID, but sometimes it may be possible to negotiate either for a lower price or to exclude utilities.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
Live in the area surrounding the uptown campus, as this is very safe and close to the university. A lot of the undergraduate (i.e. college) students live on the side towards Broadway St and this side is generally more noisy. The side towards Calhoun St is more calm, and consists mostly of families and graduate students  

The university does not recommend that you sign anything before you have seen the apartment. We took a leap of faith and it turned out great, but I know that a lot of people had poor houses and/or bad roommates.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was a bit stressful to find housing on your own, but there is a lot to choose between so it was not too difficult.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Course registration happened through Gibson (their version of KUnet), which was easy to use.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
The actual courses that were offered was not clear until getting access to Gibson. It was possible to read the course catalogue prior to that, but it consisted of courses that were only offered offered at certain times (e.g. only spring term, every third year, etc.), which was not clear. 

The system is different than at UCPH. Firstly, because securing a spot on a course can depend on how quick you are at registering. If you do not make it on the list while there are open spots you can apply to be on the waitlist. A lot of people change their courses, so it's very likely to get a course even when you're on the waitlist - unless it's a seminar, as they have fewer spots available. 

Secondly, there is an "add and drop period" in the first couple of weeks where you can try your courses and change them if you don't like them. This was nice, as you could get to learn the professors teaching method, the exam form, etc. It was not possible to find the exam form before the courses started. We were told early on that as a main rule international students get an extra 20 min for every hour of an exam, unless it's a 24 hour take home exam or a paper.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The university was very accommodating. They were always quick to answer any questions. I know that at least two courses added spots, as there was students that couldn't get the course, but there was some instances where it was not possible to add spots (e.g. seminars).

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
Two of the courses that I initially wanted were not available in the fall term. One of them were only available in the spring term and the other was only available every third year.

There were a lot of other courses that I liked, so in the end I was very happy with my courses. The courses that i signed up for had a lot of available spots, so there was no issues with securing a spot.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Register as soon as you get access to Gibson. You can only register for a specific amount of credits, so prioritize to register for the courses that you really want or the ones with fewer available spots (e.g. seminars).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The law school was very good. The courses were interesting and the teachers were very engaged.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
The level was much higher than I expected, but it was not as hard as at UCPH. The 1L courses generally seemed to be easier than the other courses. 

There was not as much pressure, as you only have to pass and it's generally easy to pass at the law school. They are not as harsh when grading as in UCPH, so the results are actually generally good. They generally try to give the exchange students as many points as possible.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The professors in the 1L courses used the Socratic method, where they would pick a random student in the beginning of the class and then only ask them questions during the rest of the class. No exchange students were called on in my 1L class, but I did hear that it happened in other classes. It can be a bit uncomfortable, but in the end it doesn't have any impact on your grade. 

In my other classes each student had to present a case throughout the term. The professors were very kind to the exchange students.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Intro to law of the US (2 credits)
International commercial arbitration (3 credits)
Admiralty I (3 credits)
Torts (4 credits)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I really enjoyed taking Intro to law of the US, as I got to know the other international students, had time to adjust the life in the US, got a very basic overview of US common law and got some cultural experiences. I could have fewer courses during the term, which I was really happy about. Although the course was a bit tiring, as we had class almost every day, class lasted for a lot of hours, we didn't get that many breaks and we got assigned readings every day. 

I took International commercial arbitration, as I wanted a course that was relevant to my future career. The course was somewhat difficult, as the class had a hard time following professor Force's teaching. 

I took Admiralty I, as Tulane is world renowned for their admiralty & maritime law program. It was a very difficult course and I would say that the level matches a course at UCPH. The course was very interesting and super rewarding when (finally) understanding it. I really enjoyed Professor Davies' teaching. Overall I'm really glad I took it, as it's made me aware of another field of law that is relevant in Denmark.

Torts is a very interesting course, especially if you like Danish tort law. Professor Gajda was really good and she made class very entertaining. She's an expert in privacy and therefore had a privacy angle on torts, which was very interesting and refreshing. The class did not have as many readings as my other classes, but it was important to attend the classes.  

Overall I would recommend all of my courses.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
I did not expect rental books from the university to be that expensive. I would recommend to buy or rent books from Amazon. 

You had to choose to get one of two health insurances through the university and it was not possible to waive either of these. It was very hard to understand what they actually covered, so I bought another Danish insurance which was a safe choice, and I'm glad I did it as the health insurance I chose didn't seem to cover much.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: The US Dollar was historically strong while I was there and inflation also became high at the same time, so everything was more expensive.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There was a lot of different events that you could participate in, which was very fun. I really enjoyed watching the sports as well.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
There was a wide range of clubs and a lot of events. The law school had several events and a lot of resources. I really enjoyed the bar reviews, where the school rented out a bar a couple of times during the term, where you got drinks and food. 

There is a gym that is mandatory to pay for, but that entails the option of doing a lot of different group exercises. 

Something that stood out was homecoming week, where there was an event every day and a very fun football game at the end. There was also great events at Halloween.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
You should definitely go see one of the parades downtown. They are very unique and super fun. If you're there in the fall term, you should see "Krewe of Boo". If in the spring, then of course "Mardi Gras". But there are other parades! 

I would recommend watching some of the basketball and football games - both at the university and downtown. 

I really liked Frenchmen St, which had the most famous jazz bars and an art market during weekend evenings. In general I would recommend exploring as much of the culture as possible. 

I was there during August, where both "Red Dress Run" and "White Linen Night" took place downtown. That was two very unique and fun events, which were definitely some of the best evenings I had. 

I also recommend going on a weekend road trip to Pensacola, Florida or Gulf Shores, Alabama. It was very nice to be at the beach and you really see another part of the south.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Watch a sports game. Go to Frenchmen St. Do a swamp tour. Take a walk in Audubon park and watch the sunset at the Fly on a Friday. Eat a Po' Boy and Beignets.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I experienced culture shock in the first couple of weeks, which I did not expect so it hit me very hard. It wore off after a bit of time, but it would have been easier to overcome if I had been prepared. I began focusing on the positive things, which there was a lot of. I thought about the negative things and tried to get a new understanding and perspective on the US system.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Participate in the events that the school offers. The first year law students are generally more interested in talking with the internationals than the other years.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: It was clear that there was some big differences between the university and the rest of New Orleans. The university has a lot of resources, which the rest of the city does not necessarily have.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The people were very open and friendly. It took some getting used to that people genuinely want to talk without having any ulterior motives.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Explore as much of New Orleans culture as possible, prioritize to plan trips and activities even when you get comfortable in a routine, and be safe.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
It was very warm outside almost all of the time, but the Americans love their AC so it was very cold inside. I would therefore recommend to bring light clothes and a sweater to wear inside. It's very cheap to buy a jacket at Goodwill if you need one. 

They don't have the best public transportation, but it's cheap. You can buy tickets through the app "RTA Le Pass". The bus is a bit shadier, but it's faster than the street car. The university also provides for some transportation. In the end i used Uber and Lyft a lot. 

I bought a bike in the beginning of the term and sold it at the end for almost the same price. I was very careful and only biked uptown, but it was nice to bike when doing grocery shopping.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: It's hard to choose: New Orleans culture, campus life, new good friends, exploring a new law system and travelling.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The US system when coming from the Danish system.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
